title: Identity-Free Deferral For Unseen Experts
one_liner: Stop teaching the AI to memorize which expert is which; instead teach it to recognize when an expert is good at a task, regardless of who they are.
lead: When a medical AI system works with human doctors, it learns to trust Doctor Alice on heart cases and Doctor Bob on lung cases. But when a new doctor (Doctor Carol) arrives, the system fails because it never learned to recognize skill itself—only to recognize Carol's face or name. This paper fixes that by teaching the system to only look at what matters: can this expert handle the confidence level of this case type?

problem.h2: The problem: teaching the AI to recognize people instead of skill
paras: Imagine you run a medical imaging lab. Your AI model looks at X-rays and makes a call: is this a tumor or normal? For hard cases, it should say I don't know—send this to an expert. You have three radiologists on staff, and they have different skills. Your model learns: when Alice is on duty, trust her judgment on lung cases; Bob handles cardiac cases; Carol knows liver cases.

Now Carol moves to another hospital, and you hire a new radiologist—Dana. Your system has never seen Dana before. It does not know that Dana is also excellent at liver cases (the same specialty as Carol). The system fails because it learned to recognize Carol specifically, not to recognize expertise in liver imaging.

callout.html: The AI learns identity-conditioned rules (Alice handles this) instead of skill-based rules (anyone skilled at this task can handle it).

panels.title: 2. The naive shortcut

panels.caption: System memorizes: Alice on duty, ask Alice; Bob arrives, ask Bob.

steps.b: Build a skill map (Bayesian competence profile)
steps.text: From a few examples, measure how well each expert handles each task type.
Feed only structural facts: model's confidence, expert's skill for this task.
Learn when to defer based solely on structural info, not expert names.
A new expert is just a new skill-profile; the rule applies without retraining.
Order of experts, order of task types—none of it matters. Only skills matter.

paras: Instead of processing expert identity (a one-hot vector saying Alice=1, Bob=0, Carol=0), the system receives only structural features: the model's confidence score for its own prediction, and the expert's estimated skill for predicting that specific task type. Identity vanishes.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Bayesian competence profile
hidden.name: Expert skill estimate per task
paras: A competence profile is a summary, built from a few examples, of how well one expert handles each task type. If Alice has seen 10 lung cases and got 9 right, her lung-competence is 0.9. If she has seen 5 heart cases and got 2 right, her heart-competence is 0.4.

The paper estimates this Bayesian competence profile (a probability distribution over possible skill levels) from limited examples. Then, when a new expert (Dana) arrives, the system runs the same estimation: show Dana a few lung cases, measure her accuracy, build her competence profile. The deferral rule now knows whether to trust Dana, because it measures skill, not identity.

heat.caption: Darker means higher skill (accuracy) in that expert-task pair. Note: Dana's lung skill (top-left corner, dark) matches Alice's.

reads.html: Skill is how often an expert gets it right. The system measures it from small examples because high-skill experts are worth asking—they will get it right more often than the AI itself will, so the AI should defer to them when the AI is unsure.
A Bayesian competence profile is a posterior distribution over expert performance, estimated from a context (few-shot batch of examples) and used to build a role-indexed state that obscures identity.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: permutation invariance by design
paras: The core insight is a symmetry property called permutation invariance. Imagine you listed all experts in a spreadsheet row: Alice, Bob, Carol. If you shuffle the row—now it is Bob, Carol, Alice—the system should still work the same way, because skill does not depend on order. Standard neural networks violate this symmetry: they learn position-specific rules (the first slot always means Alice, the second slot always means Bob). Identity-Free Deferral fixes this by using only stateless, positional-agnostic features: not the expert's index or name, but their Bayesian competence profile and the task at hand.

When a new expert Dana arrives, the system estimates her competence profile the same way, using the same Bayesian machinery. The deferral rule—which says defer when (model_confidence is low AND expert_skill is high)—applies unchanged. Dana is not a new slot or a new identity; she is just a new skill profile, and the rule is blind to identity so it works immediately.

The mechanism is a permutation-invariant encoder. Instead of building a vector like [Alice=1.0, Bob=0.0, Carol=0.0, Dana=0.0], the system builds [task_type_skill=0.8, model_confidence=0.3, ...]—a signature that describes the situation, not the person. The deferral decision logic now sees only the situation.

stages.s: New expert arrives, give her a few task examples
Measure accuracy per task type—build Bayesian competence profile
Feed into deferral rule (trained on old experts, but identity-free)
Defer or decide, generalized to unseen expert

math.h2: The math: identity-free state and permutation invariance
math.words: The state vector contains only role-indexed features, and the deferral policy is a function of this state that respects permutation symmetry.
symbols: how sure the AI is about its own prediction (0 to 1)
probability this expert gets this task type right, estimated from examples
how spread out the model's confidence is among its top predictions (higher means less certain about which class is right)
the complete information fed to the deferral decision rule

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Case: AI predicts lung nodule with 60% confidence. Expert Alice has 90% accuracy on lung cases.
State contains: 0.6 (how confident AI is), 0.9 (how often Alice succeeds on lung cases), 0.4 (how scattered the model's top predictions are), plus other structural info
Old system would also store Alice's position slot, making a larger vector that encodes: I am Alice in slot 1, Bob is slot 2, Carol is slot 3
New expert Dana arrives with same 90% lung accuracy. Her state contains: 0.6, 0.9, 0.4 (identical structural features!)
The trained policy sees the same state, so it defers with the same confidence. No retraining needed.
Old system fails because it never learned what to do when an unknown expert (no slot assigned) arrives.

math.note: The state ignores who the expert is and focuses only on whether they are skilled for this task type.

charts.title: Naive expert-conditioned deferral
charts.note: System learned to recognize specific experts, so new ones are treated as unknown.

charts.title: Identity-Free Deferral (IFD)
charts.note: System learned to recognize skill patterns, so new experts with the same skill transfer immediately.

items.b: Competence profile estimation fails with too few examples.
items.html: If Dana only handles 2 cases during onboarding, the skill estimate is noisy. The deferral rule then gives unreliable guidance. The fix: use Bayesian estimation (which models uncertainty) and require enough onboarding examples.

items.b: Task types must be stable across experts.
items.html: If your task categories shift (lung cases suddenly mean something different), the Bayesian profiles no longer align. The fix: define task types consistently before deploying the system.

items.b: Expert skill may not be truly permutation-invariant.
items.html: In the real world, Alice might be better than Dana at lung cases even if both show 90% accuracy in the test set—because Alice has intuition that doesn't show in small data. Permutation invariance assumes the true skill distributions are exchangeable, which can fail in small data regimes. The fix: use larger onboarding sets or accept limited generalization.

items.b: Done right: small onboarding set, consistent task definitions, validated skill estimates.
items.html: When the Bayesian competence profiles are accurately estimated and task types are truly stable, the identity-free representation generalizes immediately to new experts.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy medical imaging task: 3 synthetic experts with known accuracies, 5 task types, and 200 labeled cases. Train a deferral policy (learn which expert to ask) using only the first two experts. Then introduce a third expert with the same accuracy profile but never seen during training. Measure deferral accuracy and compare against a baseline that learns identity-conditioned policies.
demo.closing: The demo must show that identity-free training generalizes to unseen experts at >80% of the accuracy of the trained experts, while identity-conditioned baselines drop below 60%.
